title: Music as an intervention to improve the hemodynamic response of ketamine in depression: A randomized clinical trial

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (left for later papers), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (the authors cite up to 20% of patients on intravenous ketamine for depression in general); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.
